blocks.h2: Basement Waterproofing

Interior drainage and a [sump pump](/northbrook/sump-pumps) work as a team: the drain tile collects the water, and the pump sends it outside, away from the house. Before recommending anything, we confirm the water is coming through the foundation and not from a leak or a sewer backup, so you don't pay to fix the wrong problem.

items.q: Who do you call when your basement floods?
items.preview: A licensed plumber first, to stop the source. Cleanup and restoration come after.
items.answer: Call a licensed plumber first. A water damage company handles cleanup and restoration, but if water is still entering your basement, the source needs to be stopped before any cleanup is effective. We identify what's causing it and make the fix. Once the water is stopped, restoration can begin.

items.q: Why does my Northbrook basement only flood in big storms?
items.preview: Big storms overload the system or overwhelm the sump. The cause decides the fix.
items.answer: In a normal rain, your sump pump and sewer line keep up. In a big storm, groundwater rises faster than an older pump can move it, or the sewer fills and pushes water back through the floor drain. We'll find out which one happened in your basement and fix that.

items.q: Is a sump pump enough to keep my basement dry?
items.preview: Only for groundwater. Sewer backups need a different fix.
items.answer: Only if your problem is groundwater. A sump pump won't stop sewage from backing up through a floor drain. If water is coming up through a drain, look at a backflow valve or an overhead sewer system instead.

items.q: Does homeowners insurance cover basement flooding?
items.preview: Often not for groundwater or sewer backup. Check your policy. We document the cause for your claim.
items.answer: Standard homeowners insurance typically does not cover flooding caused by groundwater, sewer backup or heavy rain. Those events usually require separate flood insurance or a sewer backup rider. If the flooding is caused by a sudden plumbing failure, like a burst pipe, your standard policy may cover it. Check your policy or contact your insurer to confirm. Our technician will document the cause, which may support your claim.

items.q: How much does it cost to fix a flooded basement?

blocks.h2: What to Do When a Pipe Bursts in Your Northbrook Home
blocks.intro: Three things limit the damage while we're on the way:

steps.body: In most Northbrook homes, the main valve sits near the water meter where the line enters the basement or utility room. Turn it clockwise until it stops.
If water is near outlets, appliances or the electrical panel, stay out of the water. Turn off power to that area only if you can reach the breaker safely.
Our headquarters is on Techny Road and our line is open 24/7. Tell us where the water is coming from and we'll take it from there.

blocks.h2: Signs of a Burst Pipe
blocks.intro: A pipe that splits inside a wall or ceiling doesn't always gush. Look for these:

bullets: Water stains spreading on a ceiling under a bathroom or kitchen.
Paint that bubbles or wallpaper that peels.
Drywall that sags or feels soft.
Carpet in a finished basement that's damp with no clear source.
Water coming out from under cabinets or vanities.
A hissing sound near a pipe.
Water spraying or dripping from a joint.
Wet spots under pipes in the basement or crawl space.
The sound of running water when every fixture is off.
A sudden drop in water pressure.

blocks.note: Seeing water come from a wall or ceiling? Shut off the main and call us 24/7, even if you're not sure it's a burst pipe.

blocks.h2: Signs a Pipe Is Frozen
blocks.intro: On a below-zero morning, a frozen pipe usually warns you before it splits:

tiles.body: If the kitchen or a bathroom over the garage gives you nothing on a frigid morning, the line feeding it has frozen somewhere.
Frost or ice on pipes in the garage, crawl space or an unheated corner of the basement means the water inside is close to freezing solid.
Ice has already stretched the pipe. It may hold while frozen and start leaking as it thaws.

blocks.note: Think a pipe is frozen? Leave the faucet open, never use an open flame to thaw it and call us before it thaws and splits.

blocks.h2: Why Pipes Freeze in Northbrook Homes
blocks.intro: The area averages about eight nights a year at or below zero, and cold snaps like the January 2019 polar vortex can last for days. These are the pipes that freeze first.

items.h3: Pipes Over the Garage and in Exterior Walls

A hose left on the spigot traps water in the line, and it freezes inside the wall. Irrigation lines that weren't blown out in fall can split too.
Galvanized steel in postwar homes and older copper are thinner after decades of use, so a freeze is more likely to split them.

items.q: How do I keep pipes from freezing in my Northbrook home?

blocks.h2: What Does a Catch Basin Do?
blocks.body: A catch basin is a box buried at a low spot in the yard or driveway, with a grate on top and a pipe leading out. Rain and runoff flow in, sand and debris settle to the bottom, and the water leaves through the outlet pipe. When the bottom fills up, debris reaches the outlet and water stops leaving. We clean the basin, clear the outlet and repair basins that have cracked or shifted.

img.alt: Diagram of a catch basin showing the inlet grate, water line, sediment settling in the sump and the outlet pipe carrying water away

blocks.h2: Signs Your Catch Basin Needs Service
blocks.intro: In Northbrook, catch basin trouble usually shows up during the first big storm of the season:

tiles.h3: Puddles That Last Into the Next Day
tiles.body: Standing water around the grate long after the rain stops means the outlet is blocked.
A full basin sends driveway and yard water the wrong way, toward the foundation.

tiles.h3: A Grate Full of Leaves and Seeds
tiles.body: Fall leaves and spring seeds pile up on the grate and wash in with every storm.
Ground settling around the basin points to a cracked or collapsing structure.

items.q: How often should a catch basin be cleaned in Northbrook?
items.preview: Once a year under big trees, less often in open yards. Clean it before spring storms.
items.answer: Basins under mature trees often need cleaning every year, ideally after the leaves drop in fall or before spring storms. Basins in open yards can go longer. If water stands around the grate after rain, it's time.

items.q: Can a clogged catch basin flood my basement?
items.preview: Yes. A blocked basin can send water toward the foundation.
items.answer: It can. When the basin can't drain, water pools in the yard or along the foundation and finds its way into the basement. Keeping it clear is one of the simplest ways to move storm water away from the house.

items.q: Should my downspouts drain into a catch basin?
items.preview: They can, if the basin and outlet are sized for it. They should never drain into the sanitary sewer.
items.answer: They can, if the basin and its outlet pipe are big enough to take the roof runoff. What they should never do is drain into the sanitary sewer, since that adds storm water to the line that carries your wastewater. We'll check how yours are connected.

bodies: Most clogged drains have an ordinary cause: hair and soap in a bathroom, grease and food in the kitchen, lint and sediment in a laundry or floor drain. We clear the clog with a cable sized for the pipe, then tell you what we pulled out and why it built up.

bodies: Kitchen sinks clog slowly. Grease, starch and coffee grounds coat the pipe a little more every day until water stops moving. Many Northbrook kitchens have been remodeled, but the drain behind the new cabinets is often the original one.

blocks.h2: What Does an Ejector Pump Do?
blocks.body: An ejector pump moves wastewater from fixtures below the main sewer line, like a basement bathroom or laundry room, up to the level where gravity can carry it to the sewer. It sits in a sealed basin, usually in the basement floor. When the wastewater reaches a set level, a float triggers the pump and it pushes everything up and out. It's often confused with a [sump pump](/northbrook/sump-pumps), which removes groundwater, not wastewater.

blocks.h2: Signs Your Ejector Pump Is Failing
blocks.intro: Catch these early, before the basin overflows into a finished room:

tiles.body: Stop using every basement fixture and call. The pump isn't keeping up.
A sealed basin shouldn't smell. Odor means a failed seal, a vent issue or a basin that isn't emptying.
If the basement toilet or shower backs up while upstairs drains work, the pump is the first suspect.
A pump that never shuts off is fighting a stuck float, a failed check valve or a worn motor.

Ejector pumps handle toilet paper and wastewater, not wipes, paper towels or grease. Those wrap around the impeller and burn out the motor.

items.preview: A sump pump removes groundwater. An ejector pump moves wastewater from basement fixtures to the sewer.
items.answer: A sump pump removes groundwater from a pit and pumps it outside. An ejector pump moves wastewater from basement fixtures, like a toilet or laundry, up to the main sewer line. They look similar but they're not interchangeable.

blocks.h2: What Is Hydro Jetting?
blocks.body: Hydro jetting clears a sewer line with a high-pressure water stream, fed through the same cleanout access point used for rodding. A specialized nozzle sprays water in every direction as it moves through the pipe, scouring grease, scale, and roots off the entire pipe wall instead of just cutting a path through the middle. It's the fix for buildup that keeps coming back after rodding, or for roots that have worked into the pipe joints. Rodding opens the line back up. Hydro jetting cleans it.

img.alt: Diagram showing how hydro jetting clears a residential sewer line, with a cross-section view of the underground pipe, jet nozzle, high-pressure water spray, and debris being flushed toward the street connection

blocks.h2: When Your Plumbing Needs Hydro Jetting

tiles.h3: The Line Needs Rodding Every Few Months
tiles.body: Fast regrowth means roots are left hanging at every joint after rodding. Jetting cuts them flush with the pipe wall.

tiles.h3: Kitchen Grease Has Built Up for Decades
tiles.body: A 1970s or 1980s kitchen line can carry 40 years of grease. It hardens on the pipe wall and narrows the line one layer at a time.
A pipe has to be clean before it can be lined. We jet the line first so the liner bonds to the old pipe.

tiles.h3: The Clog Keeps Coming Back After Rodding
tiles.body: Rodding breaks through the immediate blockage, but it leaves buildup on the pipe walls that the next clog catches on. Hydro jetting clears what rodding leaves behind.

blocks.h2: Does Your Northbrook Basement Need an Overhead Sewer?
blocks.intro: Some homes back up once in a decade. Others back up every big storm. Here's how to tell which group you're in, from mild to severe:

tiles.h3: A Little Water at the Floor Drain in Big Storms
tiles.body: Water rises around the floor drain during a downpour and drains away by morning. It's easy to ignore, and it's usually the first sign your connection can't keep up.

tiles.h3: The Line Is Clear, but It Still Backs Up
tiles.body: The camera shows no roots and no damage, yet the basement takes on water every heavy storm. That points to the connection itself, not a clog.

tiles.h3: You've Already Lost a Finished Basement
tiles.body: Carpet, drywall and furniture ruined by sewer water once is enough. Another temporary fix isn't worth round two.

blocks.h2: How an Overhead Sewer System Works
blocks.body: Every drain below the street sewer's flow line, like your floor drain, a basement bathroom, or a laundry line, normally relies on gravity to reach the sewer. An overhead sewer system reroutes those drains into a sump pit instead. An [ejector pump](/northbrook/ejector-pump) lifts that wastewater up to a line above flood level, where a check valve keeps it from flowing back down. From there, gravity carries it the rest of the way to the street sewer, the same as every drain upstairs.

blocks.h2: Overhead Sewers and Northbrook Basements
blocks.intro: Northbrook has a long flood history, and many of its homes were built with basements that drain by gravity alone.

items.body: The September 2008 floods and the April and June 2013 storms put water into Northbrook basements, and 2018 brought flooded streets and underpasses. If your floor drain backed up during any of them, the next big storm will likely do the same.

items.h3: Finished Basements Have the Most to Lose
items.body: If your lower level is finished, with carpet, a bathroom or a bedroom, a single backup can cost more than the conversion that would have stopped it.

items.h3: How a Conversion Works in Your Home
items.body: We reroute the basement drains to a sealed pit. An [ejector pump](/northbrook/ejector-pump) lifts the wastewater up through the foundation wall, where it flows to the street by gravity. If the sewer backs up, the water has nowhere to go but back down its own pipe.

items.h3: Keep Storm Water Out of the Sanitary Line
items.body: Drain tile and downspouts should never be tied into the sanitary sewer. We check for those connections during the assessment, because they add storm water to the line you're trying to protect.

blocks.h2: Overhead Sewer vs. Sump Pump vs. Backwater Valve

blocks.h2: What to Do During a Sewage Backup
blocks.intro: A sewage backup is a health risk as much as a plumbing problem. Here's what to do while we're on the way:

steps.body: Don't flush, run the dishwasher or do laundry. Every gallon that goes down a drain has nowhere to go but back up.
Sewage carries bacteria. Keep everyone out of the affected area and don't try to clean it with bare hands.
Our phone line is open around the clock, including weekends and holidays. Tell us which drains are backing up and we'll take it from there.

blocks.h2: Why Sewage Backs Up Into Northbrook Homes
blocks.intro: Most backups we see in Northbrook come down to one of these. The camera tells us which:

tiles.h3: Roots in an Older Clay Line
tiles.body: Homes built between 1940 and 1969 often have clay sewer pipe. Roots enter at the joints and build a mat that catches everything else.

tiles.h3: A Storm That Overloads the System
tiles.body: During heavy rain, extra water enters the sewers through cracks and leaky joints. When the system fills, sewage takes the lowest way out, often your floor drain.
Grease hardens in the line, and so-called flushable wipes don't break down. Together they close a pipe one layer at a time.
If a basement bathroom drains through an [ejector pump](/northbrook/ejector-pump), a failed pump backs up sewage even when the main line is clear.

blocks.h2: Sewage Backups in Northbrook Homes
blocks.intro: Northbrook backups tend to cluster around storms. The September 2008 floods, the April 2013 storm that hit while the ground was still frozen and the June 2013 storm all sent water into Northbrook basements.

items.body: When heavy rain falls on frozen or soaked ground, almost none of it soaks in. More water reaches the sewers at once, and the risk of a backup goes up.

blocks.h2: Why Northbrook Sewer Lines Fail
blocks.intro: Northbrook was built in two big waves. About a third of today's homes went up between 1940 and 1969, and another third in the 1970s and 1980s. Each wave has its own sewer problems.

items.body: Ranches and split-levels from the 1950s and 1960s usually drain through clay pipe laid in short sections. After 60 years of ground movement, those joints open up. Roots get in, and the line starts catching paper and grease at every gap.

Newer homes aren't in the clear. A line installed in 1978 is now close to 50 years old. We often find cracked fittings, sagging sections where the soil settled after construction, and joints that were never sealed tight.

When storms hit Northbrook, like the June 2013 storm that dropped more than three inches and brought about 165 flood calls to the Village, groundwater seeps into cracked pipe. A damaged line fills faster and backs up into the lowest drain in the house.
Postwar subdivisions were planted with trees that are now 60 years old or more. Their roots follow moisture straight to the sewer line and keep growing once they're inside.

blocks.h2: What Is Sewer Rodding?
blocks.body: Sewer rodding clears a blocked main line with a long, flexible steel cable fed through a cleanout access point. A cutting head on the end breaks through roots, grease, and debris and pushes the blockage toward the street connection, restoring flow through the pipe. It's the standard first fix for a clogged or backed-up sewer line. For most homes, it's the only fix needed.

blocks.h2: When You Need Sewer Rodding
blocks.intro: A plunger fixes one fixture. These signs point to the main line under your house and yard:

tiles.h3: Water Comes Up Through the Floor Drain
tiles.body: The floor drain is the lowest opening in most Northbrook basements, so a main line blockage shows up there first. Stop running water and call.

tiles.h3: The Washer Backs Up the Basement
tiles.body: In many split-levels, the laundry drains to the lower level. If the floor drain overflows when the washer empties, the main line can't take the flow.
A toilet that bubbles when the tub drains means air is being pushed back through the system. That's a main line clog, not a toilet problem.

tiles.h3: You Rodded It Last Year Too
tiles.body: If the line needs rodding every year, roots or a damaged joint are growing back between visits. The camera shows which.

blocks.h2: Why Northbrook Main Lines Clog
blocks.intro: Most of the main line clogs we clear in Northbrook come from the same two places: the clay joints in postwar homes, and the trees that grew up around them.

items.body: About a third of Northbrook homes were built between 1940 and 1969, many on clay sewer pipe. Roots squeeze into the joints, form a mat and catch everything that flows past. Rodding cuts them back and gets water moving again.
A partly blocked line can handle a normal day. During a heavy storm, when extra water is moving through the system, it can't. That's why many Northbrook backups show up in the middle of a downpour.

If roots return within months, [hydro jetting](/northbrook/hydro-jetting) cleans the whole pipe wall. If the camera shows a cracked or separated joint, a [sewer repair](/northbrook/sewer-repair) is the fix that lasts.

blocks.h2: What Is Trenchless Sewer Repair?
blocks.body: Trenchless sewer repair, also called no-dig sewer repair, fixes a damaged pipe without digging a trench along its full length. Instead of opening up your yard from the house to the street, we work through one or two access points and repair the pipe from the inside or replace it in place. There are two main methods: cured-in-place pipe (CIPP) lining and pipe bursting. Both fix the line underground, so what's above it stays untouched.

img.alt: Two J. Blanton plumbers setting up sewer camera and cable equipment beside a home's foundation before a trenchless sewer repair

blocks.h2: Why Trenchless Fits Northbrook Homes
blocks.intro: Northbrook homeowners tend to stay put: about 87% of homes are owner-occupied. When you've spent years on a lawn, a patio or a driveway, a repair that skips the trench is worth asking about.

items.body: Many Northbrook homes sit back from the street on wide lots, so the sewer runs a long way under lawn, walks and plantings. Lining or bursting the pipe in place leaves all of it alone.

items.h3: Postwar Clay Is a Good Candidate
items.body: Root-cracked clay joints from the 1950s and 1960s are exactly what lining is built for. The liner seals every joint at once, so roots have nowhere to get back in.
A trench along the line cuts through the same roots you'd like to keep. Working underground protects the trees on your lot and on the parkway.

blocks.h2: How Trenchless Sewer Repair Works in Northbrook
blocks.intro: Both methods replace the work of a trench. Which one we recommend depends on what the camera shows.

When the old pipe is too broken to line, we pull a new pipe through it while a bursting head breaks the old one apart. The line is replaced end to end without a trench.

blocks.h2: Signs Your Water Heater Needs Repair
blocks.intro: Water heaters usually warn you before they quit. Here's what Northbrook homeowners call us about most:

tiles.h3: Hot Water Runs Out Halfway Through a Shower
tiles.body: Sediment takes up space in the tank, or a burner or element isn't heating fully. In a house with three or four bathrooms, you notice fast.
A drip at the drain valve or relief valve is usually a repair. Water coming from the tank body means the tank has failed.
That's sediment on the bottom of the tank boiling as the burner heats through it. Flushing helps if it's caught early.
On a gas heater, a dirty or failing thermocouple or flame sensor will shut the burner down. It's a common, fixable repair.

blocks.h2: Water Heater Problems in Northbrook Homes
blocks.intro: The median Northbrook home was built in 1976. Water heaters last about 8 to 12 years, so many homes here are on their fourth or fifth heater, and many of those heaters are working harder than the first one ever did.

items.body: Homes from the 1970s and 1980s often have more bathrooms than the original heater was sized for, especially after a remodel. A heater that's too small runs nonstop and wears out sooner.
The area sees about eight nights a year at or below zero. Incoming Lake Michigan water is at its coldest then, so the heater runs longer to keep up. That's when a weak heater gives out.
Most heaters here sit in a basement or utility room, often next to a finished space. A slow leak can soak carpet and drywall before anyone notices, so a drip at the base is worth a call.

blocks.h2: Residential Water Heater Service
bodies: We service the heaters found in Northbrook homes: gas and electric tank heaters, power-vent units, and tankless heaters in basements, utility rooms and garages. blocks.h2: Water Heater Maintenance and Flushing
bodies: Every tank collects sediment. As it builds up, the heater takes longer to heat, makes more noise and wears out sooner. A flush clears it out. While we're there, we check the anode rod, the relief valve and the burner or elements, so a worn part gets replaced before it turns into a leak.

Most manufacturers recommend flushing a tank about once a year, and tankless units need regular descaling. If your heater has never been flushed and it's more than a few years old, start with a maintenance visit before you assume it needs replacing.
